doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

title: Live tapes from the Armadillo and the Antilles deal
summary: Recording the quartet live in Austin, releasing two LPs on small labels, then negotiating records with Ron Goldstein at Antilles.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: It didn’t happen overnight. I used to get friends together to record, we had friends in the studios that you know, had engineer friends and stuff and be able to get into the studio after midnight and record for free and then do things on spec and things like that, and I started taking more control over that. And I just got to know it better but then when Phil’s producer was no longer a producer I had been recording our group when we were on the road. I had recorded several hours of performance at the venue in Austin, Texas called the Armadillo World Headquarters. Great venue, and mostly like rock and western swing and country music, you know, Texas music. But they had jazz groups there. We had a great booking agent. He would book us in places like that. And they loved us there. And they had a recording studio behind the stage and I recorded the band for, you know, twice I think in subsequent years, maybe ’78, ’79. And I had these tapes, they were beautiful, beautiful-sounding tapes. The guys were wonderful engineers, direct to two track live recording which became kind of my trademark. It was, you know, old school recording, which is, I am from that school.

Well we had them but we had been dropped by RCA. We did not have a record deal. I had the tapes and somehow word got around about them and these two small labels, one was in Baltimore, one was in Washington. They called me and they wanted to do a thing with two albums, that I had enough material for two LPs. So they split it up. One took one and the other took the other. They are, “Phil Woods’ Quartet Live” and “More Live”

they were called. They were the first records that I got production credit on. And you know we went from making — you know I was able to negotiate you know a fairly nice budget for those. They were already recorded and I hadn’t spent a lot of money recording them so I was able to get probably a total of maybe 15 grand for both of them and then the next thing that happened was Ron Goldstein from Island Records called me because I had met him when he was with Warner Brothers Records. And he was starting out as president of an Island subsidiary, an Island subsidiary called Antilles Records, which sounds like your “Aunt Tilly” but it was Antilles. Like the Lesser Antilles.

And we had talked about — he liked us but he couldn’t sign us to Warner Brothers. But in any case he called me and he said, “What are you doing, what’s happening with the group?” I said, “Well we’re available.” He said, “Well I want to sign you guys for a couple of records.” So he did and those paid, the first one paid $13,500 and the second was $15,000. So I negotiated that. And then the guys in the group started to think maybe Bill really knows how to produce records. Actually I had the gift of gab man. I could like go in and got to know these people and I started hanging with these people. I got to know presidents of record companies and you know agents and promoters and all of that, and I was an active player. And I was producing one of the great jazz groups, which I happened to be the drummer in. Another fortuitous circumstance.
